newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-HAEGGMAN STILL TO HIT THE HEIGHTS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-HAEGGMAN STILL TO HIT THE HEIGHTS.

text.p: When Joakim Haeggman became the first Swede to be selected for the European Ryder Cup team in 1993, he felt it was the next step on his inevitable path to stardom.
But despite a victorious Cup debut when he won his singles match on the last day, Haeggman has never achieved the heights he felt he was headed for.
A dislocated left shoulder sustained playing ice hockey late in 1994 proved to be a setback from which he has never fully recovered.
Yet on Wednesday he gave a clue as to why he had attracted such praise by shooting a course-record eight-under-par 63 to snatch the lead at the Loch Lomond World Invitational.
Though he achieved it on a still, calm summer morning which rendered the 7,050-yard course virtually defenceless, he still had to make the putts.
He required only 27 of them, making it the first time since the first round of the British PGA Championship late in May that he had gone round in less than 33 putts.
It was not his first 63 this year. He had one in the second round at the Cannes Open in April to recover from a first-round 83 and enable him to make the halfway cut.
"But this one contained three dropped shots and on a course of this quality is was probably one of my better rounds," Haeggman said.
When then-Ryder Cup captain Bernard Gallacher picked him in 1993, he said he felt he had unearthed a new star.
Haeggman did not disagree. "Until then I never had any doubts or thoughts that the next year would not be better than the previous one," he said on Wednesday.
"Though 1994 was not great I just looked at it as a bit of an off year but then after the hockey injury 1995 was a big blow to me."

"The shoulder jumped out and jumped back in again and I thought I might be out a couple of weeks. Then after a week I went out jogging and I could hardly breathe. That's when we discovered two cracked ribs as well."
He feared losing his playing card in 1995 until six top 10 finishes helped him keep it. He finished 40th on the money list, then dropped to 60th last year.
This year he is 88th with six missed cuts in 14 events including his last three.
The injury still causes him problems and three or four times a year he has to take painkillers.

"I have tried and tried and it is a vicious circle because you think you are perhaps trying too hard and it doesn't happen. You have been used to playing to win tournaments and suddenly you are just trying to finish 30th.
"You lose steam, you want to win, you want the blood to pump in your veins again, but it doesn't happen. You are standing there like it is Monday afternoon."
Though he feels his ambitions have been thwarted, he has not abandoned hope.
"Golf was everything in my life, everything I have dreamed of doing. All I wanted to do was hit golf balls. I went to bed and just wanted to get up again and hit more golf balls," he recalled.
The combination of injuries and lack of success was hard to accept.

"Before that, everything was so easy," Haegmann said. " I could only see victory. I still have a chance of coming out of this stronger. It feels like I still haven't missed the train. It is still something to jump on. I am not even 28 yet."
